sections.html:
• Scientific name: Cardisoma armatum
  • Other names: African rainbow crab, Rainbow crab, Indigo crab, Land crab, Moon Crab, Patriot crab, Tricolor crab, Harlequin crab, Halloween Land Crab, Soapdish crab
  • Type: semi-terrestrial crab
  • Minimum tank: 20 gallons (80 litres)
  • Breeding: very difficult
  • Carapace size: 7–12 cm
  • Aquarium type: paludarium (an aquarium with both terrestrial and aquatic elements, freshwater)
  • KH: 2–10
  • Humidity: 75% and higher
  • Nitrate: less than 20 ppm
  • Diet: omnivorous
  • Temperament: aggressive
  • Life span: up to 8 years
  • Colour: purple-blue carapace and orange-red legs

Rainbow Crabs are a popular group of semi-terrestrial crabs. They are hardy and easy to care for. Cardisoma armatum is not a fully freshwater species. Adult Rainbow crabs are semi-terrestrial (land) crabs and need water only to moisten the surface to refresh their gills.

Rainbow Crabs are land crabs that originate from the West Coast of Africa. They can be found along coastal regions in river deltas and other brackish areas, building homes near sources of fresh water or seawater.

Their homes are burrows in sand that grow deeper and more complex as they age. Though in nature they can build deep colonies of tunnels, in captivity male Rainbow Crabs become territorial in the presence of other male crabs.

Keep Rainbow Crabs in a water-tight aquarium of at least 20 gallons (80 litres) per crab. As adults, one male and one female may be kept together in the same aquarium of 40 gallons (150 litres) or more, but two adult males would need far more space to prevent territorial fighting.

Make sure none of the elements in the tank reach high enough for the crabs to crawl out. Rainbow Crabs are excellent climbers and will escape given the opportunity. If the tank is short, or the elements inside are too tall, tightly fasten a lid to the tank to prevent the crabs from escaping and becoming injured.

Rainbow Crabs can grow fairly big in aquariums. Naturally they reach 15 cm long, but they are likely to be nearer 7–12 cm when kept at home. The total weight can range between 96–290 g, so it is better to give them extra space in case they grow larger than expected.

Rainbow Crabs need an aquarium that has both terrestrial and aquatic elements (paludarium). A freshwater tank with only a rock or driftwood to climb out onto is not suitable. In scientific literature they are usually called land crabs, and some have been found several kilometres from the coast.

Land vs water ratio

Provide freshwater or brackish water (around 5–10%); there is no difference and they do fine in both. The environment should be 10–30% water so the crabs can keep their gills wet and molt properly. The water should be free from chlorine and other harmful chemicals.

Water bowl and water type

Instead of a complex setup, you can use a big water bowl, big and deep enough for the crab to get in and completely submerge. Water changes are then easy and no filter is needed.

For brackish water, never use simple aquarium salt or table salt; use marine salt such as Instant Ocean. For freshwater, bottled spring water is suitable; tap water is the last choice. Use Seachem Prime to remove chlorine and chloramine; it also binds heavy metals, ammonia, nitrites and nitrates for up to 48 hours.

Substrate

The rest of the tank should be filled with a mixture of moist sand or mud for burrowing, plus pebbles, river rocks or other material the crab can use to climb into and out of the water. The substrate should be damp enough to hold its shape when squeezed, but not so wet that it drips or pools water ("sandcastle consistency"). A mixture of cocofiber and sand is the best option, though each can be used alone. Provide at least 5 cm, ideally 7–12 cm of substrate, with stones, cork bark and other hides.

Tip: test the consistency by sticking a pencil all the way down and pulling it up. If the tunnel does not collapse, the substrate is fine.

Spray the substrate regularly with fresh dechlorinated water to keep it moist. Never use saltwater to maintain moisture, as salt does not evaporate and builds up harmfully.

Large rocks give the crabs a dry place to rest. They also need caves or shadowy areas to hide when frightened or to molt safely.

Humidity

Humidity is vitally important. The crabs breathe through gills, and oxygen exchange depends on the humidity of the air. If the air is too dry they will suffocate. They need a relative humidity of around 80 percent. Crabs dig less when their gills are moist. Too high humidity is not desirable either, as it causes condensation and encourages bacteria and fungus.

Molting

Molting is essential and decisive for growth in weight and size. During molting, Rainbow Crabs absorb a lot of water until the carapace opens at a breaking point, then wriggle out of the old shell. If it goes well, it takes 5–30 minutes. The molted shell looks like a dead crab but is hollow. Do not remove it: it contains a lot of calcium and other microelements, and the crab will eat it afterwards.

The crab should be left alone during this vulnerable time. Calcium is needed to harden the shell. Depending on age, they molt from every few weeks to several months. Before molting they stop eating (sometimes for weeks) and become more sluggish.

Tip: some experienced aquarists do not recommend feeding after molting until the crab has eaten its old shell and restored calcium balance, as in nature.

Optimal pH 7.0–7.5, KH 2–10, GH 12–22, nitrate less than 20 ppm, humidity 75% and higher (around 80% relative humidity is needed). Rainbow Crabs prefer a warm habitat: a tank kept at 24–29°C is within the correct range.

Cardisoma armatum can tolerate a maximum loss of body water of 20%, which developed in 3–4 days without water and resulted in a 25–30% increase in hemolymph osmolality. Within 24 hours of rehydration, they return to the original levels.

Heaters and any other electronic elements should be carefully hidden or placed out of reach, so the crabs cannot interfere with them while exploring. Rainbow Crabs have very strong claws and can even damage metal cords; hide everything or they can short circuit across the contacts.

If a big water bowl is used, no filter is needed.

Rainbow Crabs are extremely opportunistic eaters and sometimes cannibalistic. They are omnivores and scavengers. They appreciate a varied diet of fruits, berries, flowers, leaves, vegetables, pellets for fish, shrimp, turtles or crabs, frozen krill, shrimp, bloodworms and insects. Creatures smaller than the crabs can become prey, and they will consume the carrion of animals that die in the tank. They may also eat live plants.

Stomach content analysis showed that they feed on plant material, crustaceans, fish fragments (bone and scales), sand grains and unidentified items. The large amount of sand grains is attributed to their burrowing nature.

Feeding rules in captivity

  • Leaves and vegetables should be the main food. Oak leaves, Indian almond leaves, walnut leaves etc. should always be available in the tank.
  • Feed once a day and remove leftovers. Rainbow crabs can drag and store food in their burrows, so check from time to time to prevent bacterial contamination.
  • Give protein-rich food only once a week, for example a piece of boiled shrimp, bloodworm, chicken, liver or fish.
  • To improve coloration, provide products such as Hikari Tropical Crab Cuisine; one of the main components is astaxanthin. The balanced formulation also promotes proper shell development.
  • Rainbow crabs need diversity in food.
  • Do not be afraid to give them fasting days to clean their digestion.

Like most crabs, Rainbow Crabs are natural loners and often become more aggressive with age. They are not social and do not need to be kept in groups; they will fight fellow members of their own species.

They are natural diggers and construct deep burrows to maintain an optimal moisture level. Although they appear terrestrial, they have modified gills and require water or high moisture to breathe.

In the wild, they are active on the land surface at night and rest in burrows during the day. They are not very timid and usually become used to their owners, and with time can adapt to a feeding schedule.

Warning: Rainbow Crabs have very strong and sharp claws and can even cut skin. Handle with care, using gloves or tweezers.

Not plant safe: they will eat, cut and uproot everything possible in the tank.

Tankmates: as they can be predatory, ideally keep them alone or with one Rainbow Crab of the other sex. They can coexist with fish, but there is always a risk of predation. Invertebrates like shrimp and snails are best avoided as they might be attacked.

Males have bright blue backs, red legs and white claws. Their underbelly apron is shaped like an upside-down T. Females typically have pale blue to grey backs, pale orange legs and white claws, and their apron is shaped somewhat like a bell. Males are more colourful than females.

Gender also shows a significant difference in the width of the shell and the diameter of the left claw, with males larger than females.

Though Rainbow Crabs can be kept in male and female pairs, breeding in captivity ranges from extremely difficult to nearly impossible. In the wild they mate on land based on lunar cycles and tides. They reach sexual maturity in approximately 3–4 years; the minimum sizes at first sexual maturity in males and females are 5.5 and 6 cm respectively.

Courtship is common (through olfactory and tactile cues). The male approaches the female with claws held high. If she is not ready, she strikes at him with her claws. If she is ready, she keeps her claws lowered and allows him to approach. The pair then engage in one to one and a half hours of preparatory behaviour, during which the female seems docile and still while the male strokes her with his legs and claws.

The appearance of eggs is preceded by molting. After mating, the female carries fertilized eggs beneath her body for 2–3 weeks. The egg cluster changes colour from orange to yellow, to gray, and finally to black. She then goes to the coast and releases them into shallow inshore waters. In the wild a female may produce 300,000–4,800,000 eggs per spawn, but very few larvae (zoea) survive. Survivors that develop into crabs must make their way back to land or they will drown.

Larval stages

Although adults tolerate brackish water and even freshwater, the larvae require salinity for successful development. Complete larval development consists of 6 zoea stages followed by a megalopa (final stage, where larvae metamorphose into tiny crabs). Depending on temperature, salinity and feeding, it takes 40–50 days from hatching to metamorphosis.

Larval size after each stage: 1st zoea 0.85 mm, 2nd 1.21 mm, 3rd 1.61 mm, 4th 1.90 mm, 5th 2.11 mm, 6th 2.41 mm, megalopa 1.54 mm. Unlike the larvae, the carapace of the megalopa becomes broader.

After a period in the plankton, baby crabs return to the mainland as megalopae or first crab stages and live in burrows deep enough to let water seep in for moisture.

Larval rearing and salinity

Larvae appear to prefer moderately brackish conditions rather than full-strength seawater. Scientists have found that larvae can survive in salinity between 15–35%. A refugium tank well stocked with microflora and fauna could potentially host the spawn.

Diet: enriched Artemia (about 10 freshly hatched nauplii/mL). Water change: daily. Aeration: gentle. Decorations: none. Light: 12:12 hours light:dark. Salinity: 15–25%. Once larvae reach stage 4, salinity should not be higher than 20%.

At this stage sand, rocks or other items reaching above the water surface are essential so the crabs can crawl to safety. A lid is also necessary to prevent escape and injury.

Before putting them in the tank, remember to acclimate the crabs. Do not confuse Rainbow Crabs with the Halloween Moon Crab or Black land crab.

Cardisoma armatum is a simple species to care for. Beginners can keep a single Rainbow Crab with few problems since they are hardy and undemanding. The biggest concern is aggression, as they may attack other crabs, fish, snails and shrimp.
